The light still swept the basin every forty seconds, though there had not been a ship in three hundred years. 

The tower stood upon the limestone scarp known as the Shelf, five hundred feet above what had once been the Straits of Malor. Down in the basin, where the water had once run deep, green, and cold enough to crack teeth, there was now only a vast crust of white salt, fractured into interlocking hexagons, punctuated here and there by the oxidized iron rib cages of dead freighters.

Kaelen trimmed the mantle with a pair of brass snips. It was an inherited habit, mechanical and rhythmic. His father had taught him the angle of the cut, and his grandmother had taught his father, back when the basin was still half-mud, full of dying kelp and desperate salvagers who strapped broad wooden planks to their boots to keep from sinking. Now, the mud was stone, the kelp was charcoal under ten feet of dust, and the salvagers were buried in the wind-scoured cemetery behind the oil cisterns.

People in the low-lying farming settlements twenty leagues inland often asked why the light was kept burning. Oil was dear; it had to be hauled up the switchbacks by mule, barrel by heavy barrel, bartered for salt-cured tubers and sheared fleece. The Guild of Watchers had dissolved during the Great Drying, its seals broken, its treasuries spent. Only the tower remained, held together by stubborn lime mortar and the simple momentum of habit.

"A light without a sea is just an insult to the sky," a travelling merchant had told Kaelen two summers back, spitting grit from between his teeth.

"A light is not for the water," Kaelen had replied. "The light is for the distance."

And distance was the only thing the basin possessed in terrible abundance. On clear nights, when the dry thermal winds blew off the interior desert, the Fresnel lens threw its four-spoke wheel of brilliance fifty miles into the dark. It swept across dunes that crept forward like slow, petrified waves. It lit the calcified prow of the *Aethelgard*, an eighty-gun galleon that had foundered on a reef three centuries before the sea decided to evaporate. It made the salt crystals sparkle like cold stars strewn across the dead floor of the world.

Kaelen lived by the cadence of the gearwork. The clockwork drive weighed four hundred pounds, suspended down the central hollow of the spiral staircase on a braided steel cable. Every four hours, he slotted the iron crank into the winch and wound it up, link by heavy link, his shoulders burning against the gravity of the earth. When wound, it ticked with a low, bone-deep thrum that vibrated through the floorboards of his bunk. If the ticking stopped, he woke instantly, his heart racing before his mind even cleared.

He kept the logbook bound in sailcloth.
*Octave 12: Wind north-northwest, carrying fine mica. Visibility twelve leagues. No movement in the trench.*
*Octave 13: Calm. Temperature dropping at midnight. Frost on the copper cowl.*
*Octave 14: The siren sounded.*

The foghorn had not blown in Kaelen’s lifetime. It was powered by a heavy leather bellows system beneath the lower gallery, designed to trip automatically only when the barometric pressure collapsed beneath a certain threshold—a hurricane warning from an era when storms had moisture enough to tear the world apart.

When the brass horn bellowed, it was not the pure note of an instrument, but a rusted, shuddering shriek that sent a flock of roosting swifts erupting from the tower eaves in panic.

Kaelen dropped his quill. He took the spiral stairs three at a time, his palm skimming the cold iron handrail until friction burned his skin.

In the lantern room, the air smelled sharply of hot oil and sudden ozone. The four-spoke beam was cutting through the dark, but the dark was no longer clear.

A front was rolling across the salt flats from the deep south. It did not look like the brown, abrasive dust storms that occasionally wandered out of the wastes. This was a wall of cloud, towering ten thousand feet into the night sky, its belly lit by the silent, violet branching of internal lightning. It had weight. It moved not with the skittering speed of dry sand, but with the rolling, majestic inertia of deep water.

Kaelen stepped out onto the iron gallery. 

The wind struck him—not hot, not dry, not smelling of dust and old lime. It was heavy, cold, and electric. It smelled of something he had only ever read about in the margin notes of old natural histories: rain on heated stone, the green musk of waking soil, the iron tang of saturated air.

He held his hand out over the railing, palm upward.

For five minutes, nothing fell except the pressure, which pushed down on his chest like a lead weight. Then, a single drop struck the back of his wrist. It was broad, heavy, and cold. It did not vanish into dust; it broke, pooling in the crease of his skin before trickling down toward his sleeve in a clear, silver bead.

Out in the basin, the beam of the lighthouse struck the deluge. 

Where the rain met the salt, the crust began to dissolve with a soft, vast, collective hiss—the sound of a billion tiny secrets being released from the stone all at once. Dry gullies that had been empty for generations began to churn with frothing runoff. In the beam’s steady path, the black skeleton of the *Aethelgard* darkened, its ancient oak timbers drinking the water, swelling, groaning as if waking from a centuries-long sleep.

Kaelen did not run down to shutter the windows. He stood with both hands locked onto the wet iron railing, his head tilted back, letting the rain wash the chalk-dust from his hair, his beard, and the corners of his eyes. Behind him, the great lens continued its steady, deliberate turn—tick, click, sweep—casting its brilliance into the downpour. 

The sea had not returned. By tomorrow noon, the clouds would tear apart and the brutal sun would bake the basin back into dry salt and shimmering mirages. 

Yet for tonight, the water ran three inches deep across the flats, catching the lantern’s sweep and throwing the light back toward the sky. Kaelen wiped the water from his brow, turned, and went back inside to wind the weights. The light, after all, had finally found its ocean.
